chunks: "A digital scope is basically a fast data-acquisition system with a clever trigger.
The probe feeds an input stage: coupling, an attenuator and a variable-gain amplifier that scale the signal to fit the ADC's range, set by the volts-per-division knob.
Then a very fast ADC samples it continuously, say a gigasample a second at 8 bits, and writes the samples into a circular memory.
In parallel, the trigger circuit watches the analog signal with a comparator against a level I set.
When the trigger condition happens, it marks that moment as time zero, the scope keeps capturing for the post-trigger time, and then stops filling.
Because the memory was already running, I also get samples from before the trigger, so I can see what led up to the event.
The processor then takes that record, interpolates between samples so the waveform looks continuous, decimates it to fit the screen, runs measurements or FFT math on it, and draws it.
The timebase just sets how fast the sampling clock runs and how long the window is.

The limits come from each stage: the front-end bandwidth rolls off high frequencies, the sample rate has to be high enough to avoid aliasing, the 8-bit ADC limits the smallest voltage step, and the memory depth limits how long I can capture at a given sample rate."
